title: Joining the musicians' union
summary: He joined the Detroit union in 1941, which had one Black representative, and heard many local trumpeters.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Then as my work progressed, the guys said, "Well, man, you're going to have to join the union," you know -- because I started working better jobs where you had to belong to the union. So that's when I first joined the union, in 1941. They had an ex-saxophone player who was the Black representative in the union, named Lanky(?) Bowman, and he really controlled that whole area, you know... [LAUGHS] But he was a great guy.
No, they only had one local in Detroit. But we had one Black representative to handle all the Black musicians! [LAUGHS] Yes...
In '41 I should have been 17. Yeah, at 17 I joined the union. So that put me, you know, into a little better class as far as for getting different kinds of jobs.

Yeah, I was still going to the Bandbox to latch on to different gigs. And I had the pleasure of hearing guys like Lester Kerr, who was a trumpet player, and his brother Gloster Kerr, and the great Cecil Lee, a trumpet player, and Russell Smith -- among some of the really great guys that I
heard playing during that period. Oh, he was a fine player. A fine player.
